papers.title: Investigating the Effects of Material Inhomogeneity on the Robustness of Magnetic Barkhausen Noise-Based Stress Characterization
papers.abstract: The Magnetic Barkhausen Noise (MBN) measurement method is widely used to evaluate stress, microstructure, plasticity and other material states of ferromagnetic materials. However, stress assessment is generally affected by material inhomogeneity or anisotropy caused by microstructure properties such as grain size, leading to low signal-to-noise ratio and poor repeatability when characterizing stress using MBN signals. In this paper, a high spatial resolution MBN sensor based on a recording magnetic head is designed. A statistical method based on grain statistics is proposed to determine the minimum number of grains required for stable MBN signals. The method is experimentally validated on fine-grained Q235 carbon steel and 27QG110 oriented silicon steel with large grains. Different feature extraction methods, including RMS, amplitude histogram and pulse height distribution of MBN signals are applied and compared for robustness of material inhomogeneity. The results demonstrate that the average effect achieved by a sufficiently large measurement area reduces the impact of material heterogeneity on MBN signals, which is particularly relevant for large-grain materials. Additionally, the normalized threshold pulse count (ThPC) feature of amplitude histogram, defined as the number of upward threshold crossings, enhances robustness to material inhomogeneity and provides good repeatability in stress characterization across materials with different microstructurual scales. Therefore, this study provides practical guidance for quantitative stress evaluation using MBN measurement.

papers.title: Influence of the Hematite/Limonite Ratio on Sinter Properties and the Underlying Microscopic Mechanism
papers.abstract: China’s iron and steel industry relies heavily on imported ores, whose hematite/limonite blending ratio markedly affects sinter strength and metallurgical properties; however, how the ratio acts through microscopic mineral phases remains insufficiently clarified. To this end, six imported iron ore fines were characterized for their high-temperature bonding phase properties (compressive strength of compacts roasted at 1280 °C), and seven gradient ratio schemes (30–60% limonite) were designed for sinter pot tests; the sinters were analyzed by XRD, optical microscopy and SEM-EDS. The bonding phase strength of hematite-type fines was on average higher than that of limonite-type fines (1364.14 N vs. 1011.15 N), although some limonite fines are heavier than some hematite fines. Techno-economic indices and metallurgical properties responded asynchronously to the ratio: the highest yield, productivity coefficient and vertical sintering speed were obtained at 45% limonite, whereas RDI+6.3 deteriorated sharply at 60% limonite (falling from 51.97% at 55% to 43.16%). Fe2O3 content first decreased and then increased with the limonite ratio, and reduction degradation was governed by the mode of occurrence of Fe2O3 rather than its total content; skeletal secondary hematite recrystallized from the liquid phase triggered crack propagation during reduction. Accordingly, limiting the limonite proportion to 40–45% (not exceeding 55%) while promoting acicular silico-ferrite of calcium and aluminum (SFCA) and suppressing skeletal secondary hematite is recommended for industrial ore blending.

papers.title: Effect of Microstructural Characteristics on the Fretting Wear Behavior of 2A70 Aluminum Alloy with Different Grain Size Grades
papers.abstract: Fretting wear behavior of 2A70 forged aluminum alloy with different grain size grades was investigated. Specimens (Grades 3.5 and 5) were tested against 42CrMoA steel at 115 °C under 40 and 240 μm amplitudes and 90–150 N loads. EBSD characterized the microstructural features, while SEM and laser confocal microscopy analyzed the wear surfaces. Grade 5 exhibited fine equiaxed grains, higher high-angle grain boundary (HAGB) density, lower second-phase content, and weaker texture. Grade 3.5 showed mixed grains, lower boundary density, and a higher unindexed fraction possibly originating from unindexed Al9FeNi particles as well as local micro-defects. At 40 μm, the microstructural effect was minor. At 240 μm, Grade 5 showed stable friction, lower wear depth, finer debris, and a continuous compacted layer. Conversely, Grade 3.5 showed fluctuating friction, higher and non-monotonic wear depth, coarse debris, and discontinuous compacted layers with microcracks. The anomalous maximum wear depth of Grade 3.5 at 90 N may be attributed to severe third-body abrasion before a protective layer forms. The superior wear resistance of Grade 5 is the result of the combined effect of multiple microstructural parameters, primarily driven by dense HAGBs, microstructural uniformity, and weak texture.

papers.title: Solidification Patterns of Ductile and Grey Cast Irons Produced from the Same Base Iron Melt: Thermal (Cooling-Curve) Analysis
papers.abstract: The cast iron foundry industry has undergone important changes in melting operations, with induction furnaces becoming a major source of molten iron. In many foundries, grey (GI) and ductile (DI) irons are produced simultaneously, including from the same base iron prepared in the same melting furnace. The response of a common base iron to the specific metallurgical treatments required for GI and DI production may differ and can be evaluated by thermal (cooling curve) analysis (TCCA). Experiments were conducted to evaluate, by TCCA, the effects of inoculation on near-eutectic DI (4.10–4.15% CE) and medium-strength GI (3.7–3.8% CE) produced from the same base iron melts, with a limited Mn content and less than 0.02% S. Based on the average values from four melts, inoculation decreased the austenite liquidus temperature by 7.2 °C in DI and 1.8 °C in GI, increased the eutectic undercooling temperature by 16 °C in DI and 2.2 °C in GI, and produced a substantially larger increase in the end-of-solidification temperature in DI. Eutectic recalescence increased by approximately 72% in both irons, while the first-derivative minimum at the end of solidification became more negative after inoculation. The results indicate that the common base iron is suitable for DI production under the specified compositional constraints for ferritic–pearlitic and pearlitic matrices. In contrast, the high degree of undercooling during solidification of the resulting GI increased susceptibility to free-carbide formation and undercooled graphite. Under the present conditions, inoculation had only a limited ability to reduce undercooling during the eutectic reaction and at the end of solidification and to promote sufficient graphitization in GI. Based on previous research on low-sulphur GI, possible improvements are recommended, including stronger inoculation, preconditioning with oxide-forming elements, a more effective inoculation technique, and/or improved graphite nucleation through an increase in the (%Mn) × (%S) factor.

papers.title: Stage-Based Total Fatigue Life Prediction of TC11 Titanium Alloy at 400 °C Considering Structural Size Effects
papers.abstract: A stage-based framework for predicting the total fatigue life of TC11 titanium alloy at 400 °C is developed by combining probabilistic crack initiation with deterministic crack propagation. A prescribed engineering crack size is used to separate crack initiation and crack propagation. The crack initiation life is derived from the measured total fatigue life and three-dimensional crack growth analysis. Structural size effects are introduced only into the crack initiation stage through weakest-link theory, using both log-normal and Weibull life distributions, while crack propagation is treated independently by fracture mechanics. Results show that crack initiation dominates the total fatigue life over the investigated loading range, and the predicted total life is relatively insensitive to the selected engineering crack size between 0.15 and 0.381 mm. Validation using disk-center simulated specimens shows that stage decomposition alone remains conservative. After incorporating the structural size effect, the Pf = 50% predictions move closer to the experimental results, with most predictions falling within a factor-of-two scatter band. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed stage-specific treatment of structural size effects in transferring fatigue life predictions from standard specimens to structural components.
